claims.text: Cryogenic deformation followed by low-temperature aging can simultaneously enhance yield strength and tensile ductility in a room-temperature-brittle MPEA.
The proposed route induces a high density of coherent nanoscale precipitates.
The proposed route induces stacking-fault tetrahedra that serve as both strengthening barriers and ductility-promoting dislocation sources.
The initial MPEA has low room-temperature ductility because of limited dislocation mobility and inadequate strain-hardening mechanisms.
The proposed processing route uses severe plastic deformation below 100 K at a deformation level greater than 50%.
Cryogenic deformation is followed by aging at 300–400°C for 1–4 hours.
The treatment produces coherent nanoscale ordered precipitates of an L12 or DO19 type.
The treatment produces a high density of deformation-induced stacking-fault tetrahedra or nanotwins.
The induced stacking-fault tetrahedra or nanotwins facilitate cross-slip and suppress localized shear banding.
Cryogenic deformation generates a high density of dislocations and stacking faults.
Dislocations and stacking faults generated during cryogenic deformation act as nucleation sites for coherent precipitates during aging.
The coherent precipitates increase yield strength through Orowan strengthening.
Stacking-fault tetrahedra and nanotwins act as reversible dislocation sources and barriers to crack propagation.
The defect structures enhance strain hardening and ductility while precipitates enhance strength.
The proposed route will increase yield strength by more than 20% relative to baseline.
The proposed route will increase uniform elongation by more than 10% relative to baseline.
Conventional aging at 600–800°C typically produces coarse precipitates that strengthen the alloy but reduce ductility through premature void nucleation and limited strain hardening.
The proposed route applies to MPEAs with moderate to high stacking-fault energy because they can generate stacking faults during cryogenic deformation without immediately fracturing.
The route may not apply to alloys with extremely low stacking-fault energy, where deformation twinning dominates without precipitate nucleation.
Failure to increase both yield strength and ductility relative to the solutionized baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
